sections.h2: What are my choices for selling a house in Hendersonville?
sections.html:
A Hendersonville homeowner can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house as it stands. The right pick depends on how much time you have, what shape the house is in, and how much you want to spend on repairs before showings.

Hendersonville sits in Sumner County, about 18 miles northeast of downtown Nashville, so many sellers are weighing a quick move against a longer marketing period at a higher price. The list below sums up each route.

  • Agent listing: best when the house is in good condition and you can leave it open for showings for weeks.
  • Sale by owner: you handle pricing, buyer questions and paperwork yourself, and a title company or attorney still prepares the closing.
  • Cash buyer: a single offer on the house in its current state, with a closing date you can negotiate.

Whichever route you choose, the deed is recorded in Gallatin and the same state recording taxes apply.

sections.h2: What is Hendersonville like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Hendersonville is the largest city in Sumner County and wraps around Old Hickory Lake on the Cumberland River. Of its 38.18 square miles, about 6.5 are water, which is why lake views and boat access show up so often in local listings.

Daniel Smith received a North Carolina land grant here in 1784 and built Rock Castle, which is still kept as a historic site. The city takes its name from William Henderson, an early postmaster. Growth picked up after Old Hickory Dam and its lake were finished in 1954, and the city is now one of the larger suburbs in the Nashville area.

State Route 386 and U.S. 31E carry most commuters toward Nashville. The Census Bureau's commute figure for Hendersonville workers is 29.7 minutes each way, so buyers often ask about drive times to Nashville. Students attend Sumner County Schools, with Hendersonville High School, Beech High School and the Merrol Hyde Magnet School among the campuses inside city limits. The Streets of Indian Lake, a mixed-use shopping area along Indian Lake Boulevard, is one of the main commercial districts.

On December 9, 2023, a tornado struck Hendersonville. If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits and inspection records together, since a buyer's lender or insurer may ask for them.

sections.h2: How do Sumner County and city taxes affect a Hendersonville sale?
sections.html:
Hendersonville homeowners receive a city property tax bill and a county bill. The city's bill also carries the residential trash fee and the stormwater charge, so the total on it is more than the tax alone.

Sumner County is on a five-year reappraisal cycle. The last one used values as of January 1, 2024, and the assessor lists the next for 2029. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, according to the Tennessee Department of Revenue. If you disagree with a value, start with an informal review by calling the assessor at 615-452-2412, then use the Sumner County Board of Equalization, which begins meeting June 1 each year.

The Sumner County Trustee at 355 North Belvedere Drive in Gallatin collects county tax. The trustee's page says interest starts on March 1 for any unpaid balance and allows up to five partial payments by check or cash. The same office runs a state-funded tax relief program for elderly and disabled owners and a tax freeze program for the county and some cities. If you are selling, ask the closing agent how the current year's bill will be split between you and the buyer.

  • Assessor, informal review: 615-452-2412
  • Trustee: 615-452-1260
  • Appeal window: Board of Equalization, June

sections.h2: What does closing cost and where is the deed recorded?
sections.html:
Tennessee charges a realty transfer tax of $0.37 for every $100 of purchase price, and a mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of debt with the first $2,000 exempt. On a $430,000 Hendersonville sale, the transfer tax works out to $1,591. Your contract says whether the buyer or the seller pays it.

Deeds for Hendersonville go to the Sumner County Register of Deeds at 355 N. Belvedere Drive, Suite 201, in Gallatin. The office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays and can be reached at 615-452-3892. It accepts electronic recording through Simplifile and CSC ERecording Solutions, which title companies commonly use. Its deed books are digitized back to 1786, and certified records run from September 1989.

The register also offers MyLandAlert, a free service that emails you when a document is recorded under your name. Sign up before and after a sale if you want a record of what gets filed against the property.

sections.h2: Can a buyer use a Hendersonville house as a short-term rental?
sections.html:
Usually not. Hendersonville's zoning ordinance defines a short-term rental as a dwelling rented for stays under 30 days, and a 2016 ordinance limits those rentals to the Old Town Commercial and General Commercial zones.

An operator in those zones needs an engineered site plan, a use and occupancy permit and a business license. A homeowner who lives in the house full time and rents only a room is not treated as a short-term rental. Rentals of 30 days or longer fall outside the restriction.

The city enforces the rule by complaint. A neighbor calls the police non-emergency line at 615-451-3838, officers inspect, and the zoning enforcement officer sends violation letters before any citation goes to City Court. If you sold a house that was being used for nightly rentals, a buyer should confirm the zoning first by calling the Planning Department at 615-264-5316.

sections.h2: Do I need a permit before I sell?
sections.html:
Before you list, find out whether any work you did needs a permit. Hendersonville runs building, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and roofing permits through its Citizen Self-Service portal, where homeowners and contractors can apply, submit plans, request inspections and pay fees.

The portal lists each inspection as pending, scheduled, passed or failed, and requests have an afternoon cutoff to be booked for the next business day. For questions, call the city at 615-822-1000.

Open or unfinished permits can slow a sale because a buyer's title company may flag them. Closing out permits you already pulled is cheaper than explaining them later. A buyer who purchases for cash can often accept a house with open items, but the price will reflect that.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hendersonville house if it needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. You can list it, sell it directly, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as is. Repairs that involve permits should be closed out or disclosed, and the price a buyer offers will reflect the work still needed.

faqs.q: Who pays the Tennessee transfer tax on a Hendersonville sale?
faqs.a: The contract decides. The state rate is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, collected when the deed is recorded with the Sumner County Register of Deeds in Gallatin, so the closing agent should show it on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for a Hendersonville property?
faqs.a: Record it with the Sumner County Register of Deeds, 355 N. Belvedere Drive, Suite 201, Gallatin, 615-452-3892. Title companies usually submit it electronically through Simplifile or CSC ERecording Solutions.

faqs.q: When does Sumner County reappraise property again?
faqs.a: The assessor lists the next reappraisal for 2029. The last one reflected values as of January 1, 2024, and appeals of a yearly assessment go to the county Board of Equalization, which meets beginning June 1.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a Hendersonville house for weekend stays?
faqs.a: Only in the Old Town Commercial and General Commercial zones, and only with a site plan, use and occupancy permit and business license. Stays of 30 days or more are not treated as short-term rentals under the city's definition.
